script.title: What Astronauts See During a Six Hour Spacewalk
script.description: Experience the extreme conditions of working outside the International Space Station through the lens of a helmet camera. From temperature swings of hundreds of degrees to the silent speed of orbit, this is the reality of extravehicular activity.

shots.narration: This helmet camera captures the perspective of an astronaut working on the exterior of the International Space Station.
To work here, astronauts wear a suit that weighs about 145 kilograms on Earth and has 14 layers.
In sunlight, the suit faces about plus 120 degrees Celsius, but in shadow, it drops to about minus 150 degrees.
A new sunrise comes every 90 minutes as the station moves through sunlight and shadow while in orbit.
Astronauts breathe pure oxygen for hours to avoid the bends because suit pressure is a third of sea level.
A spacewalk usually lasts six to eight hours while the crew works on the exterior of the station.
More than 270 spacewalks have been made to build and repair the station since its construction began.
A small jetpack called SAFER is worn by the astronaut in case a safety tether fails.
The first spacewalk was performed by Alexei Leonov in March 1965 and lasted only twelve minutes.
